text: The embassy comes in by the Mingde Gate at the hour the street drums stop, and Zhuque Avenue opens ahead of it, a hundred and fifty paces wide and perfectly empty. Red banners hang from every ward wall the whole length of it, each at the same height, each the same distance from the next, gold characters on red: WITHOUT THE GREAT TANG THERE WOULD BE NO NEW CHINA. SERVE THE EMPEROR. THE GREAT TANG DREAM. EIGHT DIRECTIONS UNDER ONE ROOF. Over the gate of the envoys’ lodging, so that no guest can miss it on the way to bed: THE GREATER CHINA CO-PROSPERITY SPHERE.

Two of the four dragons are not Han at all. The Red Dragon is Ashina She’er, a prince of the Turkic royal clan who keeps his felt tents inside the capital walls; the White Dragon is Qibi Heli, who brought his whole Tiele tribe over the Wall as a boy. The steppe calls the Second Emperor the Heavenly Qaghan, and he answers to it. His six favourite chargers came off the steppe too, and one of them carries a Turkic prince’s title for a name. The Black Dragon is the empress’s brother, Zhangsun Wuji, who argued against this war in council and is riding to it anyway.

So the armies divide. Sun Renshi, Liu Renyuan and the king of Silla take the land road to Juryu. The Black Tortoise takes the water: a hundred and seventy warships and the grain boats, down the Ungjin river toward the White River, with Du Shuang beside him and, on the same deck, Buyeo Yung.

One fortress does not hear it. At Imjon, Ji Subsin shuts the gate and holds through the autumn, and Silla’s siege breaks on it and goes home in the eleventh month. It falls in the end to Baekje hands. Heukchi Sangji and Satek Sangya, who held the hills for Boksin, come over to the Tang, and the Black Tortoise gives them back their armour against Sun Renshi’s advice and points them up the slope.

In Sabi markets they spit when they say Sword of the Divine Country. In Surabol they toast it. In both cities someone always adds, quietly, that Hundred-Victories Gyebek has not yet been measured against him — and until Yellow Mountain, the title Greatest Blade of Samhan remains a tavern argument with two correct answers.

At the Battle of Gwansanseong (관산성) in 554, Silla’s armies kill King Seong (#26) of Baekje — the man who had, only a year before, helped Silla take the Han River from Goguryeo. The man who orders that killing is the Cloud King — Jinheung (#24).

King Mu of Baekje sends spies — five hundred armoured men under General Uso — to slip through Jade Gate Valley (옥문곡, Okmun-gok) and bite Doksan Fortress in the dark. Queen Sunduk reads the omen in a pond of toads and sends steel instead of prayers.

The outpost is also a building site. Three summers ago the Tang levelled the mound of Sui bones at the Liao, the one Goguryeo had heaped up as a trophy, and the court took the hint: every commandery now owes the crown men and stone for a chain of border forts strung a thousand li from Buyeo Fortress down to the sea at Bisa, so that the next emperor who comes east has to climb a wall every day of his march. The court calls it the Thousand-Li Wall. The men hauling the stone just call them the Eastern Fortresses. When Yeon is not killing anybody he walks the new courses with a plumb line and kicks the blocks that are not square.

Meanwhile the rest of the line comes down like roof tiles, and the Tang clerks file it in a single column. At Baegam Yeon sends the Ogol garrison out to break the siege, and they put a spear into the White Dragon’s waist; he has it bound and is back in the saddle by evening, and the lord of Baegam, Son Daeeum, opens his gate anyway. Out on the southern cape the emperor’s fleet takes Bisa in a month. Of the forts Yeon spent fourteen years hauling stone for, only Sinseong and Geonan still fly Goguryeo banners.

Munmu names nineteen generals to deal with it. One of them is Kim Jinju, Grand General of the Tang Army Command, a True Bone of good family who led men at the Yellow Mountain and has a son serving in the emperor’s guard at Chang’an.

In the second month of 664 the Tang name a Commander of the Bear Ford Commandery: Buyeo Yung, Euija’s crown prince, who knelt in front of Bupmin’s horse at Sabi and was spat on, and then went to Chang’an and came back in Tang robes. He is to govern what is left of Baekje on the emperor’s behalf, from the fortress where his father was arrested.

The Taehak (태학), the Grand Academy, has stood in the capital since the second year of King Sosurim, and it arrived in the same season as the first Buddha images from the Former Qin. The academy and the temple came over the river together and have shared the noble sons of Goguryeo ever since: the Five Classics in the morning, sutras after the midday meal, archery whenever the masters lose their voices.

High Councillor Supum has held the first chair since Euljé left it. The Harmony Council’s six sleeves — Alchun, Yushin, Murim, Imjong, Suljong, and Bidam — still decide only by unanimity, which is the only way the Council selects anything.
King Pungjang (37) · Gwishil Boksin · Hukchi Sangji · Satek Sangya · Bagon · Echi no Takutsu

The imperial envoy Liu Renyuan presides. The Black Tortoise has written the oath. On one side of the altar stands King Munmu of Silla. On the other stands Buyeo Yung, Commander of Bear Ford, whose face Munmu last saw at the height of his horse’s knees.

High Councillor Bidam (53) — Second Blade of Samhan — and Yumjong raise men at the Fortress of Radiance (명활성). The slogan is already old; they only give it a banner. Yumjong holds the outer muster while Bidam walks the rampart as if the stones owed him rent. Inside Wolseong the stewards count the grain and arrive at ten days. Nobody says the number aloud. Everybody schedules by it. The rebel band ties black headbands — Bidam’s old colour from the yard — so the fortress can tell its own from Wolseong’s blue.

Across the floor the Sword of Silla — Kim Yushin — catches the Second Blade’s eye — Bidam — Gaya-blood marshal’s grandson and the boy from one of Surabol’s oldest halls, trading wins since they were Hwarang. The count stands at one hundred and eight apiece. Neither has ever let the other stay ahead for long.

In 551, Baekje under King Seong and Silla under Jinheung — the Cloud King — with Gaya contingents — push Goguryeo out of the Han River basin. The understanding is clear enough for wartime: Baekje will keep the lower reaches, nearer the sea; Silla will take the upper valley.

Kim Seohyeon is the son of the last prince of Golden Gaya, which in Surabol is the kind of fact people bring up just after he has left the room. His father Muryuk handed the kingdom over and then spent the rest of his life proving it had been a bargain: on the Gwansan road he took a king of Baekje, four of that king’s generals and ten thousand heads. The family is True Bone now. The rank opens most doors in the capital, and it opens the best ones least.

Seohyeon rises the way a Gaya man rises in Surabol, one rank at a time, each one signed by someone who remembers the box. By the end he is a sopan, third rank in the kingdom, and Governor-General of Daeyang Province, the south-western march that faces Baekje, with its seat at Daeya Fortress. Yushin’s memorial stone will give his father a different name, Soyeon, and the historian, unable to decide between them, writes both down and moves on.

Count the banners before the water does. Tang comes by sea, twice. Liu Rengui, the Black Tortoise, has held the old Baekje capital at Ungjin for two winters with a garrison too small to be called one, and when an imperial letter told him he could come home, he wrote back that he would rather not. In the spring the emperor sends Sun Renshi across the Yellow Sea with seven thousand more. The Silla annals, which like round numbers, make it four hundred thousand.
Silla is a class society dominated by the Bone Rank System (골품제), where everything is determined by one’s rank. There are the 6 Common Ranks, and then the Nobles and Royals.
Yeon prepares to head to Pyongyang for the High Summit (제가회의), a gathering of all Five Commanderies (오두) of Goguryeo, in his father’s place.

At Dokseongsanseong (독산성) and along the river the allied banners still fly together. Then, in 553, the Cloud King turns his army on the Baekje share. He seizes the lower Han, installs a new province — Sinju (신주) — and staffs it with men who will not ask what the alliance once meant.

The letter goes to King Bojang rather than the Mangniji. Mamok Pass and Jungnyeong were Goguryeo’s land to begin with, it says, and once Chunchu is home he will ask his own sovereign to give them back. He signs it with a flourish. He has no intention of doing any such thing, and Seon Dohae, finishing the jar, has no intention of mentioning it.

In the Tang line, among the guard captains, is a man whose Chinese still has the sea in it. Sul Gedu left Silla twenty-four winters ago in the hold of a merchant ship, and when the emperor called for men to march on Goguryeo he put his own name forward, which is the only way a foreigner becomes a captain of the Left Militant Guard. Across the field the Goguryeo banners are close enough to read.

At Najeong well in Yangsan the horse knelt and cried; the six chiefs — Alpyung, Sobuldori, Jibekho, Gurema, Jita, Hojin — dug where it stood and lifted a great egg. The shell opened on a boy already kingly in the face. He learns fast. The chiefs say the land has been waiting.

Seventh month heat sits on the Yellow Mountain like a second army. Dust rises white off the three roads. Downstream, past ground Hundred-Victories will never see again, Tang sails already crowd the White River mouth — the Red Fowl’s host waiting for the inland door to open. Hwangsan is that door.

When Sabi fell the Tang drew five commanderies over Baekje like a net over a pond, and put the largest of them at Bear Ford on the Geum, Ungjin, where Euija had been handed over. So far the net catches mostly rebels.

The White Tiger drives into the Snake River with a Tang host that still believes rivers are roads. Yeon Gesomun has been waiting for a man who thinks that. Old men in the north still say Salsu when they mean a river that eats armies; the Snake is younger, hungrier, and has Yeon’s name on its teeth.
The Blue Dragon, with the Black Tortoise and White Tiger II, lead the Tang forces.

Hanseul is past twenty. He has carried Kim Yushin across the Yellow Mountain Fields, through the snow to Pyongyang, and back over the Imjin with Goguryeo’s horsemen behind them. His muzzle has gone grey, which on a white horse nobody notices except the man who feeds him.

Hwanung lands on a mountain under a sandalwood tree — 신단수, the divine birch — and names the ground beneath it Sinsi, the Divine City. Three thousand followers come with him; among them the Earl of Wind, the Master of Rain, and the Master of Cloud. Someone has to argue with the weather.

Marshal Yushin (37), Sword of Silla, Munhee’s older brother, is unusually close with Princess Dukman. He is the leader of the Hwarang, an elite training corps for young noblemen — horse, bow, and the gyuku field where Surabol decides who matters before the court does.

King Seong feels the cut in the marrow. He gathers Baekje, remaining Gaya houses, and a Wa contingent promised by the Yamato court, and in 554 marches on Gwansanseong — the fortress that opens the road into Silla’s throat.

Sinseong, the New Fortress, does not fall; the emperor’s cousin, the Prince of Jiangxia, spends ten days under its walls and comes away with nothing. So the Blue Dragon leaves a guard to watch it and turns south, and Gaemo goes in a little over ten days. Seven hundred men Yeon sent down from Gasi to hold it are taken in the gate. They ask to serve the emperor instead.

Between the Six Armies and the walls lies the Liao marsh, two hundred li of mud where a Sui host once went in to the knee and came out as a song. The Master of Works, Yan Lide, lays earth across it in a road wide enough for carts. When the last wagon is over, the Second Emperor has the road torn up behind them. Nobody is going home the way they came, and he wants every man in the column to know it.

At the Battle of the Colossal River — Salsu, in the mouths of those who fought there — the general Ulchi Munduk decisively defeats the Western Army. A century later men will still point at other rivers and hope for the same appetite.

The names already know the argument, if anyone cared to listen. Bidam and Sadaham sound like this soil and its sutras — sadaham is a station on the Buddhist path, the once-returner. Yushin (庾信) and Chunchu (春秋) are names a Chang’an clerk could file without asking; Spring and Autumn, like the classic. Nobody notices yet. Names are patient.
The Cloud King — Jinheung, greatest of Silla’s kings — along with Sadaham, God of the Hwarang, conquers Gaya in the year 562.

The chest of court robes that came home from Chang’an is opened in the first month of the next year. By spring every official in Surabol above a certain rank has been measured for one. The year after that Silla stops counting its own years and starts counting the emperor’s, and Bupmin sails west with Queen Jinduk’s Ode to Great Peace woven into a length of silk, which the Third Emperor admires extravagantly.

King Muyeol comes as far as Geumdol Fortress and no farther: the field belongs to his son and to Yushin. He sends fifty thousand men west under Kim Yushin with a date in their heads. Between them and the date is the pass at Tanhyeon, and beyond the pass, a man called Gyebek.

Outside Sabi, on the twelfth day of the seventh month, the Silla army reaches the Tang camp two days after the date it was given. The Red Fowl has the Silla commissary officer, Kim Munyeong, brought to the gate of his tent and his collar opened for the sword.

On the third day of the ninth month the Red Fowl sails for home with Euija, his sons, and twelve thousand captives, leaving Liu Renyuan with ten thousand men to hold Sabi beside a Silla army that has stopped smiling at him.

Before long an edict comes to Surabol naming the new king, Munmu, Grand Commander of the Gyerim Prefecture. Gyerim is the old name of Silla, the wood where the first Kim was found in a golden box under a crowing white rooster. In the edict it is a prefecture of the empire, and the king of Silla is its governor.

The courier carrying the news finds Xue Rengui a thousand miles the other way, under the Tianshan, where he has just ended a war against the Tiele with three arrows and his soldiers are already singing about it. He is given the dead man’s title — White Tiger II — and the job of settling the account.

The annals are not finished with him. Eight years later the same pages have a Jinju sent to behead Suse, governor of Hanseong, who was caught arranging to go over to the Tang commandery in Baekje, and later tellings like that version better and give him the credit for putting down the rising at Naesaji as well. Either Silla had two men of the name, or a clerk killed him once and forgot. The one person who never mixes the versions up is his son.

Upriver at Juryu, King Pungjang still believes a kingdom can be restored by enough sails. Over three summers the East has sent him a thousand ships, by the count Silla will later send the Tang, and some forty-two thousand men — Echi no Takutsu among the captains who still say Kudara. They come down on the eighth month’s water, packed too tight for oars, shouting for a victory the tide has already priced differently.

The Silla court hears the name and goes very quiet. Silla men died at the Yellow Mountain Fields for this ground. The Second Emperor promised it to Chunchu by lamplight. Now it has a Baekje prince on it again, holding a Tang seal.

In the eighth month of 665, on a hill outside Bear Ford that the Tang clerks write as Chwirisan, the Mountain Where One Goes for Gain, the empire makes the two men who rule the south swear to be brothers.

In Surabol the anger is louder. Silla men bled at the Yellow Mountain Fields, at Sabi and in the snow outside Pyongyang for land the emperor promised them, and now they have sworn on a dead horse never to take it. The young officers say the word betrayal in the barracks. The older ones say nothing, and start counting Tang garrisons.

Han takes Wanggeom in 108 BC. Some of the people the king told to live go south over the mountains and settle in six villages in the valleys around Surabol, where, two generations later, they will go looking for a king. The rest stay, and are cut into the Four Commanderies of Han. The last of them, Nangnang on the Taedong, is still collecting taxes four hundred years later.

In the seventh month of 671 a Tang monk named Imyun is rowed ashore under a white flag with a letter from the fleet. The fleet belongs to Xue Rengui, White Tiger II, who has been sitting off the coast all summer and would prefer, if it can be managed, to win this war by post.
The thirteenth Eraha of Baekje bestows the Seven-Branched Sword (칠지도) to the King of Wa, as a symbol of friendship.

He took the throne at seven and reigned thirty-six years. By the end of them Silla held the Han River basin, the east coast up toward the Malgal country, and Gaya. He got there by being the most reliable ally in Samhan — right up until the afternoon he wasn’t.

What the Assembly votes on, more often than war, is water. Who may load first at the western wharves. Whose ships may winter in the White River mouth. Which house takes the Tamla orange levy, and which takes the Yamato silk berth. In Baekje a clan without a harbour right cannot feed a fight.
At the Siege of Pyongyang, Baekje’s King Geunchogo (#13) kills Goguryeo’s King Gogukwon (#16).

The summons is not addressed to him. The Eastern Commander is still his father, Yeon Taejo, who sat the High Command in Pyongyang for twelve years, came home to the east when his brother Gusesa took the chair, and is now too old to sit a horse as far as the capital. The son has done the work for years. The seal is still the old man’s.
At the Siege of Hansung, Goguryeo’s King Jangsu (#20) kills Baekje’s King Gaero (#21).

The Yeon family lives in Pyongyang these years, in the big house below the palace hill, because the High Commander is Gesomun’s father, Yeon Taejo. He has held the chair for ten years, long enough to outlive most of the men who voted for him and none of the ones who voted against. Most nights he comes home from the Summit in a silence the servants have learned to walk around.

Euija learns the Eight Great Clans at his father’s table, and Chunchu learns the Harmony Council from the way it walked his grandfather off the throne and kept his father waiting outside its doors. Yeon Gesomun learns Pyongyang here, from an old man reading the same report three times by lamplight because nobody else in the city would read it once.

That is where the name comes from. Not from Surabol, which likes its titles stamped and filed, but from the people he beat: Goguryeo calls him the Sword of Silla first, and means it as a warning. On the eastern border mothers use it for a generation to get children indoors before dark. Thirteen years later, when the Eternal General hears that the same sword is riding for a Silla prince in his prison, he remembers a hall in Pyongyang, a report read twice, and his father reading it a third time.

Then the Eastern Fortress itself: Yodong, the city that held the Sui off for three summers and never opened. The Blue Dragon has already driven one sortie back through its gate when the emperor arrives. He rides to the edge of the moat, carries a sack of earth across his own saddle and throws it in, and his officers, who cannot be seen carrying less than the Son of Heaven, carry two. The Tang ring the walls a hundred deep and beat the drums until the ground answers.

When the dust settles, the two Goguryeo commanders, Go Yeonsu and Go Hyejin, walk into the Tang camp with thirty-six thousand men behind them and surrender. The officers are sent inland, to be Tang subjects somewhere far from any border. The common soldiers are sent home. The three thousand Mohe riders who came south with them are marched into a valley and buried alive.

The Guardian of Ansi Fortress is an eccentric man. After Yeon’s Massacre he refused the Eternal General to his face and kept the old king’s colors on the wall — and Yeon, who had drowned a court for less, looked at that wall, weighed the siege, and rode away. Ansi answers to no one.

Kim Muryuk, prince of Golden Gaya, had already surrendered his kingdom to Silla in 532. His grandson is Kim Yushin, the great general of Silla. Before the hall, the field. The tall Gaya cone still fights.

The boy grows up at the edge of things, in county houses on the Goguryeo road, with a younger brother, Heumsun, and two sisters the household calls by their baby names, A-hae and A-ji. They will grow up to be Bohui and Munhui and to cause a great deal of trouble over a skirt.

Since the Ministry of War cannot find him a general, Chunchu tries the Historiography Office. Chu Suiliang receives him among the shelves: the man who once refused to let the emperor read his own diary, now high enough at court to choose what he says and careful enough to say very little.

They have watched him work. In the border years after Daeya, Gyebek earned the name Hundred-Victories mostly one way, and the Silla garrison towns learned to dread it. He leaves the line to other men and goes looking for the general. Gomanari, the black horse from the Gomanaru ferry, is the fastest thing on four legs in Samhan, and Gyebek rides him flat along the neck like a thrown knife, the blade reversed back along his forearm. The general sees a black shape where the field was empty, starts to turn his horse, and does not finish turning. One cut on the pass. By the time the escort draws, the black horse is a speck on the far ridge and an army is standing in a field with nobody left to tell it what to do.
Onjo and Biryu grow up princes of Goguryeo, Jumong’s sons by Sosuno, and nobody in Jolbon mentions Buyeo.

In the sixth month of 660 he sails from Shandong with a hundred and thirty thousand men and drops anchor off Deokmul Island. A Silla fleet of a hundred ships comes out to meet him. At its head is the crown prince, Bupmin, thirty-four years old and trying not to stare at the size of the Tang flagship.
Ye Sikjin, the guardian of Bear Fortress, captures Euija and surrenders to the Red Fowl.
King Muyeol finally arrives at the scene. He makes Euija pour his wineglass, and the Red Fowl’s beside it, and executes the traitors Gumil and Mochuk.

In the ninth month Yeon Namseng holds the Yalu with several tens of thousands. The river freezes overnight. Qibi Heli, the White Dragon of the old war, walks his army across the ice at dawn with the drums going, and kills thirty thousand men who had been guarding a river that was no longer there.

In the twelfth month a letter reaches Surabol from the Tang camp. The Red Fowl is out of rice. King Munmu reads it out to his generals, and nobody offers, because everyone in the room knows what the road north looks like in the twelfth month. Kim Yushin, who is sixty-six, offers.

Before Boksin and the king there were Boksin and the monk. Dochim raised the first restoration banner at Juryu with him in the autumn Sabi fell, a monk who put down the begging bowl for a spear and named himself General of the Spirit Army. For a year the two of them held the west between them, and the Tang garrison at Sabi could not go out for water.

The Black Tortoise has already learned the river’s grammar: narrow mouth, sandbars that shift like lies, a current that punishes anyone who charges without forming line. He anchors a hundred and seventy ships across the throat of the White River and waits. On the east bank Kim Yushin’s land army keeps the shore from becoming a pier.

The Black Tortoise has seen men of Wa once before, four years ago in Luoyang: an embassy in court silk that bowed in all the right places, and that the court then kept in a guesthouse for two winters so it could not carry home the news of where the fleet was going. These are the embassy’s cousins. They row standing up, they shout at a range where shouting does nothing, and they come straight at a hundred and seventy anchored hulls in boats built for rice. No army of the Middle Kingdom has fought them before today. He watches the first wave break on his line the way a scholar reads a script he has never seen, looking for the grammar.

Silla settles him at Geumma, south of the old Baekje capital, in a town that was Baekje’s until ten years ago. Within the year he is styled King of Goguryeo; four years later, King of Bodeok, and in time he is given a Silla bride and a seat at Munmu’s feasts, well below the king’s.

In 674 the Third Emperor strips King Munmu of every Tang title and names a new king of Silla: Kim Inmun, Munmu’s younger brother, who has lived in Chang’an since he was a young man of twenty-two and has to be told by an official that he is going home with an army.

Liu Rengui, the Black Tortoise, is given the army. Inmun is given the title, a new robe in the Silla colour, and a seat in the general’s ship that faces backwards, toward Chang’an. The Tang clerks are very particular about where a puppet sits.
Xue Rengui comes back by sea in the ninth month, with a Silla man named Kim Punghun as his pilot — the son of a man Munmu executed, showing the Tang fleet the way into his own coast.
